summary: How the body builds and breaks down its main hormones: thyroid hormone, adrenal steroids, catecholamines, insulin, and the posterior pituitary peptides. Exam questions name a blocked enzyme or an odd lab pattern and ask you to predict what builds up, what falls, and what the patient looks like.

points: The sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) on the basolateral membrane pulls iodide into the follicular cell using the sodium gradient; TSH increases it.
Pendrin carries iodide across the apical membrane into the colloid.
Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) uses hydrogen peroxide to oxidize iodide and attach it to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin (organification), forming MIT and DIT.
TPO also couples them: DIT plus DIT makes T4, and MIT plus DIT makes T3.
For release, TSH drives endocytosis of colloid; lysosomal proteases cleave thyroglobulin and free T4 (most of the output) and some T3.
Leftover MIT and DIT are deiodinated so the iodide is reused; peripheral 5'-deiodinase turns T4 into the more active T3.
ACTH drives cholesterol into mitochondria through StAR protein, the rate-limiting transport step.
Side-chain cleavage enzyme (desmolase, CYP11A1) converts cholesterol to pregnenolone, the parent of every steroid.

Zona glomerulosa lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase, so it makes aldosterone: progesterone, then 11-deoxycorticosterone (21-hydroxylase), corticosterone (11-beta-hydroxylase), aldosterone (aldosterone synthase).
Zona fasciculata uses 17-alpha-hydroxylase: 17-hydroxyprogesterone, then 11-deoxycortisol (21-hydroxylase), then cortisol (11-beta-hydroxylase).
Zona reticularis uses 17,20-lyase to make DHEA and androstenedione.
Block rule: substrates above a blocked enzyme pile up and spill into the pathways that are still open, and low cortisol raises ACTH, which drives even more flow.
Tyrosine hydroxylase (rate-limiting, needs tetrahydrobiopterin) converts tyrosine to L-DOPA.
DOPA decarboxylase (needs vitamin B6) makes dopamine; dopamine beta-hydroxylase (needs vitamin C and copper) makes norepinephrine inside vesicles.
PNMT adds a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to make epinephrine; cortisol arriving through the adrenal portal flow from cortex to medulla induces PNMT.
COMT converts epinephrine and norepinephrine to metanephrine and normetanephrine; MAO then makes vanillylmandelic acid (VMA). Dopamine breaks down to homovanillic acid (HVA).

Pheochromocytoma cells metabolize catecholamines to metanephrines continuously, so plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines are the most sensitive tests even when catecholamine release is episodic.
Preproinsulin is made on the rough ER; removal of the signal peptide gives proinsulin (B chain, C-peptide, A chain), which folds and forms disulfide bonds.
In secretory granules, prohormone convertases cut out C-peptide, leaving insulin (A and B chains joined by two disulfide bonds).
Insulin and C-peptide are released in equal molar amounts; the liver clears much of the insulin on first pass, while C-peptide is cleared by the kidney and lasts longer.
Pharmaceutical insulin contains no C-peptide, so high insulin with low C-peptide means injected insulin.
Both are made in magnocellular neurons of the supraoptic nucleus (mainly ADH) and paraventricular nucleus (mainly oxytocin).
Each is made as a larger precursor that includes its carrier protein, neurophysin; the pair travels down the axons of the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract by axonal transport.
They are stored in axon terminals in the posterior pituitary and released by calcium-triggered exocytosis when the neurons fire. The posterior pituitary stores these hormones but does not make them.
The mineralocorticoid receptor binds cortisol about as well as aldosterone, and free cortisol circulates at far higher levels.
11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 in collecting duct cells converts cortisol to cortisone, which does not bind the receptor, so aldosterone stays the main signal.

Glycyrrhetinic acid in licorice inhibits this enzyme; cortisol then activates the receptor, causing sodium retention, hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis with low renin and low aldosterone.
The same pattern appears with inherited loss of the enzyme (apparent mineralocorticoid excess) and when huge cortisol levels overwhelm it, as with ectopic ACTH.

tricks.label: Starts with 1 means hypertension; ends with 1 means virilization
tricks.text: 11-beta-hydroxylase starts and ends with 1 (hypertension and virilization). 17-alpha starts with 1 (hypertension, no virilization). 21 ends with 1 (virilization, no hypertension).

tricks.label: Hydroxylate, decarboxylate, hydroxylate, methylate
tricks.text: The four steps from tyrosine to epinephrine in order: tyrosine hydroxylase, DOPA decarboxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, PNMT.

tricks.label: C-peptide only comes from the patient
tricks.text: Any source that makes the patient's own beta cells secrete (tumor or sulfonylurea) raises C-peptide with insulin. Insulin from a vial raises insulin alone.

highYield: TPO does both organification and coupling; antibodies against it mark Hashimoto thyroiditis.
T4 is the main secreted hormone; T3 is the active one, made mostly in peripheral tissues by 5'-deiodinase.
StAR transport of cholesterol into mitochondria is the rate-limiting step in steroid synthesis.
21-hydroxylase deficiency raises 17-hydroxyprogesterone, the newborn screening marker for congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme for catecholamines; cortisol induces PNMT.
Plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines are the best screening tests for pheochromocytoma.
High insulin with low C-peptide means exogenous insulin.
Licorice causes a low-renin, low-aldosterone hypertension with hypokalemia by blocking 11-beta-HSD2.
pitfalls: 11-beta-hydroxylase and 21-hydroxylase deficiency both virilize. Hypertension and low potassium point to 11-beta, because 11-deoxycorticosterone builds up and acts as a mineralocorticoid.
In 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency, the extra mineralocorticoid is mostly 11-deoxycorticosterone; aldosterone itself is often low because renin is suppressed.
Sulfonylurea use and insulinoma give the same insulin and C-peptide pattern; only a drug screen separates them.
Licorice and primary hyperaldosteronism both cause hypertension with hypokalemia, but aldosterone is low with licorice and high in primary hyperaldosteronism.

summary: The genetics behind endocrine disease: tumor syndromes, inherited enzyme defects, diabetes genetics, thyroid cancer mutations, and disorders of sex development. You also need to know how steroid and thyroid hormones act as transcription factors. Questions give a family history or a karyotype with hormone levels and ask for the gene, the inheritance, or the mechanism.

points: MEN1: loss-of-function mutation in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene, which encodes menin.
A person with MEN1 inherits one bad copy in every cell; a tumor forms only after a second hit knocks out the normal copy in a gland cell.
MEN2A and MEN2B: gain-of-function mutation in the RET proto-oncogene, a receptor tyrosine kinase. One mutant copy is enough to drive growth.
Both are autosomal dominant: each child of an affected parent has a 50 percent chance of inheriting the mutation.
RET carriers are offered early prophylactic thyroidectomy because medullary thyroid carcinoma develops in nearly all of them.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is autosomal recessive; carrier parents have a 25 percent risk of an affected child each pregnancy.
About 90 to 95 percent of cases are 21-hydroxylase deficiency from CYP21A2 mutations; the gene lies in the HLA region on chromosome 6.
Type 1 diabetes is linked to HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 (and the DQ alleles inherited with them).
Type 2 diabetes is polygenic, with no HLA link, and has higher monozygotic twin concordance than type 1.
MODY is monogenic and autosomal dominant: young onset, not obese, no autoantibodies, not ketosis prone.
Glucokinase MODY resets the beta cell glucose sensor higher, giving mild, stable fasting hyperglycemia; HNF1A MODY (a common type) worsens over time.
Papillary carcinoma: BRAF V600E point mutation (most common) or RET/PTC rearrangement (linked to radiation exposure); both switch on the MAP kinase pathway.
Follicular carcinoma: RAS point mutations or PAX8-PPARG fusion.
Medullary carcinoma: RET point mutations, germline in MEN2 and familial cases, somatic in many sporadic tumors.
Anaplastic carcinoma often adds TP53 loss on top of an earlier BRAF or RAS mutation.

Androgen insensitivity: X-linked androgen receptor defect in a 46,XY person. Testes make testosterone and AMH, so there is no uterus, but the body cannot respond to androgen and the external genitalia are female.
In androgen insensitivity, testosterone and LH are high (no feedback); breasts develop from aromatized testosterone, and pubic and axillary hair is scant.

5-alpha-reductase deficiency: autosomal recessive, 46,XY, low DHT with normal testosterone; ambiguous external genitalia at birth, normal Wolffian structures, and virilization at puberty when testosterone rises.
Klinefelter syndrome 47,XXY (meiotic nondisjunction): small firm testes, infertility, gynecomastia, tall stature; low testosterone with high LH and FSH (primary hypogonadism).
Kallmann syndrome: GnRH neurons fail to migrate from the olfactory placode with the olfactory neurons, giving anosmia with low GnRH, low LH and FSH, and delayed puberty (secondary hypogonadism).
Steroid hormones and thyroid hormone are lipid soluble and cross the cell membrane to reach intracellular receptors.
Steroid receptors such as the glucocorticoid receptor wait in the cytoplasm bound to heat shock proteins; hormone binding releases them so the receptor can dimerize and move to the nucleus.
The thyroid hormone receptor sits on DNA in the nucleus as a heterodimer with the retinoid X receptor; T3 binding swaps corepressors for coactivators.

The receptor's zinc finger domain binds a hormone response element and turns genes on or off, so effects take hours to days and last longer than the seconds-to-minutes effects of peptide hormones acting through second messengers.

tricks.label: MEN1 has 3 Ps, MEN2A has 2 Ps, MEN2B has 1 P
tricks.text: MEN1: parathyroid, pituitary, pancreas. MEN2A: parathyroid and pheochromocytoma (plus medullary thyroid cancer). MEN2B: pheochromocytoma only (plus medullary thyroid cancer, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus).

tricks.label: Where the problem is tells you LH and FSH
tricks.text: If the testis fails (Klinefelter), the pituitary shouts: LH and FSH go up. If the signal never arrives (Kallmann), LH and FSH are low.

tricks.label: Receptor problem or enzyme problem
tricks.text: In 46,XY with female or ambiguous genitalia, check DHT. Normal testosterone with low DHT is the enzyme (5-alpha-reductase). High testosterone, high LH, and normal DHT is the receptor (androgen insensitivity).

highYield: MEN1 is a tumor suppressor (two hits needed in the tumor cell); RET in MEN2 is a proto-oncogene (one hit is enough).
Both MEN syndromes are autosomal dominant.
Most congenital adrenal hyperplasia is autosomal recessive 21-hydroxylase deficiency from CYP21A2 mutations.
Type 1 diabetes: HLA-DR3 and DR4. Type 2: polygenic, with higher twin concordance than type 1.
BRAF V600E and RET/PTC point to papillary carcinoma; RAS and PAX8-PPARG point to follicular; RET points to medullary.
Kallmann syndrome is low GnRH with anosmia; Klinefelter is 47,XXY with high LH and FSH.
The thyroid hormone receptor pairs with the retinoid X receptor on DNA.
pitfalls: MEN1 is inherited as a dominant trait even though the gene is a tumor suppressor that acts recessively in the cell. Inheritance pattern and cellular mechanism are different questions.
Androgen insensitivity and 5-alpha-reductase deficiency are both 46,XY. Androgen insensitivity has no virilization at puberty and scant body hair; 5-alpha-reductase deficiency virilizes at puberty.
Twin concordance in diabetes runs opposite to what many students expect: it is higher in type 2 than in type 1.
Thyroid hormone acts through a nuclear receptor even though it is made from amino acids. Group it with steroids.

A second somatic hit to the normal copy is needed for a tumor
Menin is a tumor suppressor (loss of function)
MEN2A cell shows one mutant RET copy that is enough on its own
RET is a proto-oncogene encoding a receptor tyrosine kinase (gain of function)
Both are autosomal dominant
MEN1 tumors: parathyroid, pancreatic neuroendocrine, pituitary
MEN2A tumors: medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia

dumps.p: Draw a target cell receiving cortisol on the left side and glucagon on the right side. Trace each hormone from the blood to its effect and write how fast each effect starts.
l: Cortisol crosses the membrane because it is lipid soluble
Cortisol binds a cytoplasmic receptor held by heat shock proteins
The hormone-receptor complex enters the nucleus and binds a hormone response element
Gene transcription and new protein synthesis follow, so onset takes hours
Glucagon binds a cell surface G protein-coupled receptor
Gs raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A
Second messenger effects start within seconds to minutes
Thyroid hormone works like cortisol but its receptor sits on DNA with the retinoid X receptor

summary: How the immune system attacks endocrine glands and how hormones and immunity talk to each other. The exam favors the mechanism behind Graves disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and type 1 diabetes, the polyendocrine syndromes, how cortisol suppresses inflammation, and why conjugate vaccines work.

points: IgG thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins bind the TSH receptor and switch it on, raising cAMP, gland growth, and hormone output.
This is a type II hypersensitivity (antibody against a cell surface receptor), here stimulating instead of destroying the cell.
TSH falls by negative feedback while T4 and T3 stay high, because the antibody does not respond to feedback.
Orbital fibroblasts and fat also express the TSH receptor; T cells and cytokines drive glycosaminoglycan buildup and swelling of orbital fat and extraocular muscles (ophthalmopathy).

IgG crosses the placenta, so a baby of a mother with Graves can have transient thyrotoxicosis that fades over weeks to a few months as maternal IgG is cleared. This can happen even after the mother's thyroid was removed.
Mainly T cell mediated: CD8 cytotoxic T cells kill follicular cells, and CD4 Th1 cells release interferon-gamma that activates macrophages.
Antibodies against thyroid peroxidase (most sensitive) and thyroglobulin are the diagnostic markers and add antibody-dependent cell killing.
Chronic lymphoid stimulation in the gland forms germinal centers and raises the risk of primary thyroid B cell lymphoma (extranodal marginal zone (MALT) or diffuse large B cell type).
Insulitis: islets fill with lymphocytes, mostly CD8 T cells, that selectively destroy beta cells and spare alpha cells.
Autoantibodies to GAD65, insulin, IA-2, and ZnT8 appear years before symptoms; they are markers of the attack, and having more of them predicts higher risk.
Symptoms begin after most beta cell mass is gone.
LADA (type 1.5) is slowly progressive autoimmune diabetes in adults: GAD65 antibody positive, at first managed without insulin, often mistaken for type 2, with C-peptide falling over time.
AIRE makes thymic medullary epithelial cells display tissue proteins so self-reactive T cells are deleted (central tolerance).
APS-1: autosomal recessive AIRE mutation; childhood chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease.
The candidiasis in APS-1 comes from autoantibodies that neutralize IL-17 and IL-22, cytokines needed for mucosal defense against Candida.
APS-2: Addison disease with autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, or both; adult onset, more common in women, polygenic with HLA-DR3 and DR4.
IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha act on the hypothalamus to raise CRH, which raises ACTH and cortisol. Cortisol then dampens the inflammation, closing the loop.
Cortisol induces annexin A1 (lipocortin), which inhibits phospholipase A2 and lowers prostaglandin and leukotriene production.
Cortisol blocks NF-kB signaling, cutting IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, and TNF-alpha output.
Cortisol lowers circulating lymphocytes and eosinophils and raises neutrophils (demargination).
Plain polysaccharide capsule is a T cell independent antigen: mostly IgM, little class switching, weak memory, and a poor response in children under 2 years.

Conjugating the polysaccharide to a protein carrier lets the B cell present carrier peptides on MHC II to helper T cells, giving CD40L help, class switching to IgG, affinity maturation, and memory, even in infants.
Meningococcal conjugate vaccines prevent invasive disease and so prevent Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

tricks.label: Graves stimulates, Hashimoto destroys
tricks.text: Graves is an antibody that turns the TSH receptor on. Hashimoto is mostly T cells killing follicles, with anti-TPO as the marker.

tricks.label: Carrier protein brings the T cell
tricks.text: The B cell sees the sugar but shows the protein. The protein peptide recruits a helper T cell, and that help is what buys class switching and memory.

tricks.label: APS-1 is candida plus two failed glands
tricks.text: Chronic candidiasis, failed parathyroids, and failed adrenals. Think AIRE and the thymus, so it starts in childhood.

highYield: Graves disease is a type II hypersensitivity with stimulating antibodies to the TSH receptor.
Transplacental IgG causes transient neonatal thyrotoxicosis in babies of mothers with Graves disease.
Anti-TPO antibody is the most sensitive marker of Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Hashimoto thyroiditis raises the risk of primary thyroid B cell lymphoma.
GAD65 antibodies mark type 1 diabetes and LADA.
APS-1 is an AIRE defect: candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, Addison disease.
Cortisol inhibits phospholipase A2 and NF-kB and lowers eosinophils and lymphocytes.
Conjugate vaccines turn a T cell independent response into a T cell dependent one with IgG and memory.
pitfalls: Graves and Hashimoto can both show antithyroid antibodies, but only Graves has stimulating TSH receptor antibodies.
Diabetes autoantibodies are markers of the attack; the beta cells are killed by T cells.
LADA looks like type 2 diabetes in an adult but is antibody positive and progresses to insulin need.
Cortisol raises the neutrophil count while lowering lymphocytes and eosinophils. Do not read the high white count as infection.

Mother has high T4 and T3 with low TSH
IgG crosses the placenta (third trimester especially)
The antibody stimulates the fetal thyroid
The newborn can be thyrotoxic with low TSH
Neonatal disease is transient and fades as maternal IgG is cleared over weeks to months
This is type II hypersensitivity

The B cell takes in the whole conjugate
Carrier protein peptides are shown on MHC class II
A carrier-specific CD4 helper T cell recognizes the peptide
CD40L on the T cell binds CD40 on the B cell, with cytokines
Class switching to IgG and affinity maturation follow
Memory B cells form, so boosters work and infants respond
Antibody plus complement prevents invasive meningococcal disease and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome

summary: The microbes that damage endocrine glands: Neisseria meningitidis and the adrenal hemorrhage of Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome, bacteria and viruses that inflame the thyroid, and the infections that destroy the adrenal cortex. Questions describe the organism or the gland damage and ask you to connect the two.

points: Gram-negative diplococcus (kidney-bean pairs), oxidase positive, ferments glucose and maltose, grows on chocolate agar.
Spread by respiratory droplets and close contact; it colonizes the nasopharynx, with outbreaks in dormitories and military barracks.
Virulence: polysaccharide capsule (blocks phagocytosis, defines serogroups), pili for attachment, IgA protease, and lipooligosaccharide (LOS) endotoxin.
The bacteria shed LOS-rich membrane blebs, so endotoxin levels in blood can be very high.
Higher risk with terminal complement (C5 to C9) deficiency and asplenia.
LOS (lipid A) binds TLR4 on macrophages and triggers TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6 release.
These cytokines injure endothelium and induce tissue factor, setting off DIC with microthrombi and consumption of platelets and clotting factors.
The adrenal has a rich arterial plexus draining into a limited venous outflow, so it is prone to hemorrhagic infarction when vessels clot and bleed.
Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage causes acute adrenal insufficiency and shock that does not respond to fluids, with a petechial or purpuric rash.
Other organisms that can cause it: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas, and staphylococci.
Acute suppurative thyroiditis is rare because the gland has a capsule, rich blood and lymph flow, and high iodide content.
Usual bacteria: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Streptococcus pneumoniae.
In children, repeated left-sided infection points to a pyriform sinus fistula, a pharyngeal pouch remnant that lets bacteria track from the pharynx to the thyroid.
Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis follows a viral upper respiratory infection; coxsackievirus and mumps are among the viruses implicated.
Coxsackievirus is a nonenveloped positive-sense RNA picornavirus; mumps is an enveloped negative-sense RNA paramyxovirus spread by droplets.
Adrenal insufficiency appears only after about 90 percent of the cortex is destroyed, and infections usually hit both glands by blood spread.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis: acid-fast rod (mycolic acid wall) that forms caseating granulomas destroying cortex and medulla; healed glands often calcify.
Histoplasma capsulatum: dimorphic fungus from bird and bat droppings in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys; small yeasts inside macrophages; disseminated disease often enlarges both adrenals.
Cytomegalovirus in AIDS: the most common adrenal infection at autopsy; cells show large intranuclear owl's eye inclusions.

charts.title: Endocrine pathogens
rows: Gram-positive cocci in clusters, coagulase positive

tricks.label: Fever, rash, shock, dead adrenals
tricks.text: A young person with sudden fever, purpura, and shock that will not respond to fluids: think meningococcemia with bilateral adrenal hemorrhage.

tricks.label: Left side, again and again
tricks.text: A child with a second left-sided thyroid abscess needs a search for a pyriform sinus fistula.

tricks.label: Painful thyroid: bacteria or virus
tricks.text: Fluctuant, tender gland with normal thyroid function suggests bacteria. Tender gland with thyrotoxicosis after a cold suggests a virus (subacute thyroiditis).

highYield: Neisseria meningitidis: gram-negative diplococcus with a polysaccharide capsule and LOS endotoxin, spread by droplets.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral adrenal hemorrhage from sepsis and DIC, classically meningococcemia.
Terminal complement deficiency predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infection.
Acute suppurative thyroiditis: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Recurrent left-sided thyroid infection in a child points to a pyriform sinus fistula.
Tuberculosis is the leading infectious cause of Addison disease worldwide.
Cytomegalovirus is the most common adrenal infection in AIDS.
pitfalls: Neisseria meningitidis ferments maltose and glucose; Neisseria gonorrhoeae ferments glucose only.
Subacute thyroiditis follows a virus, yet the gland shows granulomas with giant cells around colloid and no viral inclusions. Caseating granulomas point to tuberculosis instead.
Cytomegalovirus adrenalitis is common in AIDS but rarely destroys enough cortex to cause Addison disease on its own.

summary: Diseases where a gland makes too much hormone: Cushing and Conn syndromes, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hyperparathyroidism, GH excess, and hyperthyroidism, plus SIADH, familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, and precocious puberty. The exam asks you to find the source from paired hormone levels and to explain each sign from what the hormone does.

points: Most common cause is exogenous glucocorticoids; the most common endogenous cause is an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease).

ACTH-dependent causes (pituitary adenoma, ectopic ACTH from small cell lung carcinoma) cause bilateral adrenal hyperplasia; ACTH-independent causes (adrenal adenoma or carcinoma, exogenous steroids) suppress ACTH, so the other adrenal atrophies with a tumor and both adrenals atrophy with exogenous steroids.
Screening: 24-hour urine free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, or failure of low-dose dexamethasone to suppress cortisol.
Then measure ACTH: low means adrenal or exogenous; normal or high means pituitary or ectopic.
High-dose dexamethasone suppresses a pituitary adenoma (some feedback is kept) but not ectopic ACTH.

Protein breakdown causes proximal muscle weakness, thin skin, wide purple striae, bruising, osteoporosis, and poor wound healing; fat redistribution causes central obesity, moon facies, and a dorsocervical fat pad.
Gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance cause hyperglycemia; hypertension comes partly from cortisol acting on mineralocorticoid receptors.
Primary: the adrenal makes aldosterone on its own, from bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (now the more common cause) or an aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn syndrome).
Findings: hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis (potassium and hydrogen ion loss in the collecting duct), with high aldosterone and suppressed renin.
No edema, because of aldosterone escape (pressure natriuresis and natriuretic peptides).
Secondary: high renin drives aldosterone, as in renal artery stenosis, heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, or diuretic use.
Primary hyperparathyroidism: single adenoma in about 85 percent; high calcium, low phosphate, and high or inappropriately normal PTH.
Effects: kidney stones and polyuria, bone pain, constipation, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, depression; most cases today are found on routine calcium tests.
Osteitis fibrosa cystica: osteoclastic resorption with fibrous replacement, subperiosteal resorption of the middle phalanges, and brown tumors (hemorrhage with osteoclast-type giant cells).
Secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD: phosphate retention and low calcitriol (lost 1-alpha-hydroxylase) lower calcium and stimulate PTH; calcium is low or normal and phosphate is high.
In vitamin D deficiency, calcium is low or normal, phosphate is low, and PTH is high.
Renal osteodystrophy is the bone disease of CKD; tertiary hyperparathyroidism is autonomous PTH secretion with hypercalcemia after long secondary stimulation, often seen after kidney transplant.

Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia: autosomal dominant inactivating calcium-sensing receptor mutation; mild hypercalcemia, normal or mildly raised PTH, very low urine calcium, usually no symptoms, and surgery does not help.
Usually a somatotroph pituitary adenoma, often a macroadenoma at diagnosis.
Before epiphyses close: gigantism (excess linear growth). After closure: acromegaly (bones and soft tissues thicken).
Acromegaly: coarse facial features, frontal bossing, prognathism, enlarged hands and feet, macroglossia, sweating, carpal tunnel syndrome, and sleep apnea.
GH opposes insulin, causing insulin resistance and diabetes; cardiomyopathy and hypertension are the leading cause of death.
Diagnosis: raised IGF-1, then confirmation by failure of GH to suppress after an oral glucose load.
Graves disease and toxic multinodular goiter both give low TSH and high free T4.

T3 raises Na-K-ATPase activity and metabolic rate (heat intolerance, sweating, weight loss with good appetite) and increases beta-adrenergic receptors in the heart (tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, tremor).
Excess thyroid hormone speeds bone turnover and causes bone loss.
Thyroid storm: fever, tachyarrhythmia, delirium, vomiting, and heart failure, triggered by stress such as infection, surgery, or delivery; it can be fatal.
SIADH causes: small cell lung carcinoma, CNS disease (trauma, stroke, meningitis), lung disease (pneumonia), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide).
SIADH labs: hyponatremia with low serum osmolality, urine osmolality inappropriately high, urine sodium high, and normal volume status.
Central precocious puberty: early GnRH activation with pubertal LH and FSH.
Peripheral precocious puberty: sex steroids from congenital adrenal hyperplasia, McCune-Albright syndrome (activating GNAS mutation), or a tumor; LH and FSH are suppressed.

rows: Carcinoma often virilizes; other adrenal atrophies

rows: Ambiguous genitalia in 46,XX; salt-wasting crisis in newborns

tricks.label: Stones, bones, groans, thrones, and psychiatric overtones
tricks.text: Kidney stones, bone pain, abdominal groans (constipation, ulcer, pancreatitis), polyuria, and depression or confusion from hypercalcemia in hyperparathyroidism.

tricks.label: Big dose, pituitary listens
tricks.text: Only a pituitary adenoma still obeys feedback at a high dexamethasone dose. If cortisol falls, it is Cushing disease.

tricks.label: Renin splits the aldosterone cases
tricks.text: High aldosterone with low renin is primary (the adrenal is acting on its own). High aldosterone with high renin is secondary (the kidney is asking for it).

highYield: Low ACTH means adrenal or exogenous Cushing; high ACTH with no suppression on high-dose dexamethasone means ectopic ACTH.
Primary hyperaldosteronism: hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, low renin, no edema.
21-hydroxylase deficiency: salt wasting, hyperkalemia, high 17-hydroxyprogesterone, virilization.
Primary hyperparathyroidism: high calcium, low phosphate, high PTH, usually a single adenoma.
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia has low urine calcium and needs no surgery.
Confirm acromegaly with high IGF-1 and failed GH suppression by oral glucose.
Ophthalmopathy and pretibial myxedema are specific to Graves disease.
SIADH: euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and high urine sodium.
pitfalls: Lid lag and stare happen in any thyrotoxicosis from sympathetic overactivity; true proptosis (ophthalmopathy) points to Graves disease.
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia can look like primary hyperparathyroidism. Check urine calcium before anyone operates.
Ectopic ACTH often lacks the classic Cushing body shape because it develops quickly; severe hypokalemia and hyperpigmentation are the clues.
In secondary hyperparathyroidism from CKD, phosphate is high; in vitamin D deficiency, phosphate is low.
A random GH level is not useful because GH is pulsatile; use IGF-1 and the glucose suppression test.

summary: Diseases where a gland makes too little hormone, or the body cannot respond to it: diabetes insipidus, adrenal insufficiency, hypoparathyroidism, hypopituitarism, and hypothyroidism, plus short stature and euthyroid sick syndrome. Most questions hinge on reading paired trophic and target hormone levels to place the problem in the gland, the pituitary, or the target tissue.

points: Central: too little ADH, from head trauma, pituitary or hypothalamic surgery, tumors such as craniopharyngioma, or infiltrative disease.
Nephrogenic: the kidney does not respond to ADH, from V2 receptor (X-linked) or aquaporin-2 defects, lithium, hypercalcemia, or hypokalemia.
Both cause polyuria with dilute urine and thirst; serum sodium rises (hypernatremia) only when the patient cannot drink enough.
Primary (Addison disease): autoimmune adrenalitis in developed countries, tuberculosis worldwide, and metastases; all three cortical zones fail.
Low cortisol raises ACTH; POMC cleavage also releases MSH, causing hyperpigmentation of skin creases, scars, and buccal mucosa.
Low aldosterone causes sodium loss, hyperkalemia, volume depletion, and hypotension with high renin.
Low cortisol adds fatigue, weight loss, hypoglycemia, and eosinophilia.
Adrenal crisis: stress in a patient with chronic insufficiency, sudden stop of long-term glucocorticoids, or bilateral adrenal hemorrhage (anticoagulation, DIC, Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome).
Cortisol is needed for vessels to respond to catecholamines, so crisis causes shock that does not respond well to fluids and pressors.
Secondary: low ACTH from pituitary disease or suppression by exogenous glucocorticoids; no hyperpigmentation and no hyperkalemia because renin and angiotensin II still drive aldosterone.
Causes: surgical removal during thyroidectomy (most common), autoimmune (APS-1), DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion, absent third and fourth pharyngeal pouch derivatives), and severe hypomagnesemia.
Labs: low calcium, high phosphate, low PTH.
Low calcium makes nerves fire too easily: perioral and fingertip numbness, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, tetany, laryngospasm, and seizures.
Chvostek sign is facial twitching when the facial nerve is tapped; Trousseau sign is carpal spasm after a blood pressure cuff is inflated above systolic pressure. The ECG shows a long QT interval.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a: maternally inherited inactivating GNAS mutation causes PTH resistance; calcium is low and phosphate high, but PTH is high. Patients have Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (short stature, round face, short fourth and fifth metacarpals).
Causes: nonfunctioning macroadenoma (most common in adults), Sheehan necrosis, pituitary apoplexy, surgery, radiation, and infiltrative disease.
Symptoms usually appear only after about 75 percent of the anterior pituitary is lost; GH and gonadotropins tend to fail before TSH and ACTH.

Primary empty sella: arachnoid and CSF herniate through a defective diaphragma sellae and flatten the pituitary; function is usually normal, but it can cause hypopituitarism or mild hyperprolactinemia.
Hypothalamic lesions (craniopharyngioma, sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, radiation) lower releasing hormones, so anterior pituitary output falls.
They also cause central diabetes insipidus, and prolactin rises because dopamine no longer reaches the lactotrophs.
Iodine deficiency lowers T4 and T3, TSH rises, and the follicles grow, first as a diffuse goiter and later as a multinodular goiter.
Features: cold intolerance, weight gain, fatigue, bradycardia, constipation, dry skin, slow relaxation of deep tendon reflexes, and high LDL (fewer LDL receptors).
Myxedema: glycosaminoglycans build up in the dermis and soft tissue, giving nonpitting swelling, a puffy face, an enlarged tongue, and a hoarse voice.
In primary hypothyroidism, high TRH stimulates lactotrophs, raising prolactin; this can cause galactorrhea, menstrual disturbance, and infertility.

Congenital hypothyroidism: thyroid dysgenesis (most common), dyshormonogenesis, or maternal iodine deficiency; babies show lethargy, prolonged jaundice, large tongue, umbilical hernia, and intellectual disability if untreated.
Euthyroid sick syndrome: severe illness reduces peripheral T4 to T3 conversion, giving low T3, high reverse T3, and usually normal TSH.

charts.title: Water deprivation test with desmopressin
rows: Low at baseline, rises with deprivation

tricks.label: The 6 Ps of congenital hypothyroidism
tricks.text: Pot-bellied, pale, puffy-faced child with a protruding umbilicus, protuberant tongue, and poor brain development.

tricks.label: Brown and salty means adrenal
tricks.text: Hyperpigmentation plus hyperkalemia places adrenal insufficiency in the adrenal gland itself. Without them, think pituitary or steroid withdrawal.

tricks.label: Desmopressin answers the question
tricks.text: If urine stays dilute after water deprivation, give desmopressin. If the kidney concentrates, the problem was missing ADH (central). If it still cannot, the kidney is deaf to ADH (nephrogenic).

tricks.label: Low calcium, then look at PTH
tricks.text: Low calcium with low PTH is a gland problem (hypoparathyroidism). Low calcium with high PTH and short fourth and fifth knuckles is a receptor problem (pseudohypoparathyroidism).

highYield: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus does not respond to desmopressin; central does.
Addison disease: hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hyperpigmentation from high ACTH and MSH.
Secondary adrenal insufficiency has no hyperpigmentation and no hyperkalemia.
Abrupt withdrawal of long-term glucocorticoids is a classic cause of adrenal crisis.
Hypoparathyroidism after thyroid surgery: low calcium, high phosphate, low PTH, Chvostek and Trousseau signs.
Pseudohypoparathyroidism has high PTH and short fourth and fifth metacarpals from a GNAS mutation.
Hypothalamic or stalk lesions raise prolactin because dopamine is cut off.
Euthyroid sick syndrome: low T3, high reverse T3, normal TSH.
pitfalls: Primary polydipsia also causes polyuria with dilute urine, but serum sodium tends to be low-normal and the urine concentrates with water deprivation.
Hyponatremia can occur in both primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency (low cortisol raises ADH), so use potassium and skin color to separate them.
Central hypothyroidism can show a normal TSH. A normal TSH with low free T4 is still abnormal.
Low magnesium causes hypocalcemia that will not correct until magnesium is replaced, because PTH release and action need magnesium.
Constitutional delay and familial short stature both grow at a normal rate. Bone age separates them: delayed in constitutional delay, normal in familial.

Secondary: renin and angiotensin II keep aldosterone normal
Secondary: no hyperpigmentation and no hyperkalemia

summary: The inflammatory diseases of the thyroid: Hashimoto thyroiditis, subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis, painless and postpartum thyroiditis, and Riedel thyroiditis. Questions give you the feel of the gland, the thyroid tests, the radioiodine uptake, or a biopsy description and ask which disease it is and how it will progress.

points: Most common cause of hypothyroidism where iodine intake is adequate; usually a middle-aged woman with a painless, firm, diffusely enlarged goiter.
Autoimmune loss of tolerance: cytotoxic T cells and Th1-activated macrophages destroy follicular cells; anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are present.
Histology: dense lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltrate with germinal centers, small atrophic follicles, and Hurthle cells (pink granular cytoplasm packed with mitochondria).
Early follicle damage can leak stored hormone and cause brief thyrotoxicosis (hashitoxicosis).
The usual course is a slow slide through subclinical hypothyroidism (high TSH, normal free T4) to permanent hypothyroidism.
It travels with other autoimmune diseases: type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, Addison disease, celiac disease, and vitiligo.
It raises the risk of primary thyroid B cell lymphoma, which shows up as a rapidly enlarging thyroid in a patient with known Hashimoto.
Follows a viral upper respiratory infection, most often in women aged 30 to 50.
Painful, tender thyroid with pain spreading to the jaw or ear, fever, malaise, and a very high ESR.
Damaged follicles leak stored hormone, so T4 is high and TSH is low, but radioiodine uptake is low because the gland is not making new hormone.
Histology: follicle destruction with neutrophils early, then lymphocytes and macrophages, and granulomas with multinucleated giant cells around pools of colloid.
Course: thyrotoxic phase for weeks, often a transient hypothyroid phase as stores run out, then recovery to normal function in most patients within months.
Painless (lymphocytic) thyroiditis: painless, mildly enlarged, nontender gland; transient thyrotoxicosis with low uptake, then often a hypothyroid phase.
Postpartum thyroiditis is the same process within the first year after delivery; it is linked to anti-TPO antibodies and can recur with later pregnancies.
Histology of painless thyroiditis shows lymphocytes without the fibrosis and Hurthle cells of Hashimoto.
Riedel thyroiditis: IgG4-related dense fibrosis that extends beyond the capsule into neck structures, giving a rock-hard, fixed, painless thyroid.
Riedel can compress the trachea, esophagus, or recurrent laryngeal nerve and mimic anaplastic carcinoma; it may occur with other fibrosing diseases such as retroperitoneal fibrosis.

tricks.label: Leaking versus making
tricks.text: Thyrotoxic with high uptake means the gland is making hormone (Graves, toxic nodules). Thyrotoxic with low uptake means the gland is leaking stored hormone (subacute, painless, or postpartum thyroiditis).

tricks.label: Sort by how the gland feels
tricks.text: Painful and tender: subacute. Painless and rubbery: Hashimoto. Painless and mildly enlarged after a baby: postpartum. Rock-hard and stuck: Riedel.

tricks.label: Hurthle cells mean Hashimoto
tricks.text: When the biopsy shows lymphoid germinal centers with Hurthle cells, it is Hashimoto. Giant cells around colloid point to subacute thyroiditis.

highYield: Hashimoto thyroiditis: lymphocytes with germinal centers, Hurthle cells, anti-TPO, painless goiter.
Hashimoto thyroiditis raises the risk of primary thyroid B cell lymphoma.
Subacute thyroiditis: painful thyroid after a viral illness, high ESR, granulomas with giant cells.
Subacute thyroiditis is thyrotoxic with low radioiodine uptake and is self-limited.
Postpartum thyroiditis is painless, anti-TPO linked, and transient.
Riedel thyroiditis is IgG4-related fibrosis that makes the thyroid rock-hard and fixed.
pitfalls: Hashitoxicosis and Graves disease can both cause early thyrotoxicosis. Graves has high uptake and stimulating TSH receptor antibodies; hashitoxicosis has low uptake.
Subacute thyroiditis is painful and has a high ESR; painless thyroiditis has the same thyroid test course but no pain and a normal or mildly raised ESR.
A hard, fixed thyroid suggests cancer first, but Riedel thyroiditis is the inflammatory mimic. Biopsy shows fibrosis without malignant cells.
